2.text: brought for the purpose. Then the noose of the lasso is arranged on the

3.text: ground so as to encircle the head of the corpse and all the objects deposited

4.text: for the use of the deceased one on the day of the funeral. Then the corpse

5.text: receives an offering from each member of the party. The remainder of the

6.text: food is spread on the stones near the dead body, and the guests partake of

7.text: it. This is considered as a meal offered by the deceased. Then the slaugh-

8.text: tering begins. If the family is rich, each of the guests will receive a

9.text: slaughtered reindeer. The poor or the avaricious kill only a few animals,

10.text: and distribute the meat among their friends; but then there will not be

11.text: such a multitude of guests. The legs of the reindeer are broken and the

12.text: marrow is extracted. The heads are cooked in large kettles, and the feast

13.text: begins, during which the corpse receives its share of all the courses.

14.text: The antlers are hewn off, as usual, with the tops of the crown, and are

15.text: burned for a few seconds in the fire to make them secure against harm by

16.text: wild beasts, which the odor of the smoke will frighten away. After that, the

17.text: antlers are arranged in a line extending from the head of the corpse toward

18.text: the direction of midnight. The antlers of each set are pointed upward, and

19.text: their bases are pressed firmly into the ground, and made fast with stones or

20.text: logs. The heap of antlers is called “antlers’ store” (tɪˊnmai). All the contents

21.text: of the paunches of the slaughtered animals are emptied on the ground, and

22.text: the iron objects left with the corpse are purified by immersing them in this

23.text: mass. Then they are taken out and carried home. In their places are left,

24.text: partly wooden substitutes, partly equivalents of inferior quality; for instance, a

25.text: splinter of bone instead of iron needles, evidently as material of which to

26.text: make bone needles, a stone scraper in the place of an iron scraper, etc.

27.text: Other objects — as cups, pipes, pouches — are not exchanged. The bow

28.text: also, as well as the iron arrows, are left in their places. Other iron objects

29.text: also are sometimes left with the corpse. I saw, for instance, iron knives and

30.text: adzes on funeral places, though, as a rule, they were old and much used, and

31.text: evidently had been given to the deceased in place of implements of a better

32.text: quality. I saw even old rifles, but they were always broken.

33.text: After the purification of the iron, the “fortifier” proceeds to the divining,

34.text: using either a special stone or any object suitable for suspension from a stick.

35.text: The details and the questions are similar to those on the day of the funeral.

36.text: The magic precautions against pursuit by the spirit are also repeated with

37.text: many variations. I saw, for instance, at one funeral at which I was present,

38.text: an old man urinate close to the head of the corpse, which astonished even

39.text: the other participants in the ceremony. His purpose was to create a river

41.text: On coming home, another feast follows, during which the piece of skin

42.text: taken from the clothes of the dead is put in the place of honor in the inner

43.text: room, and receives its share of the food. This is repeated at every meal
